Toward the Era of Agentic Embodied Intelligence

Abstract

Frontier foundation models can increasingly guide robot actions, but sustained physical autonomy also requires efficient control and recovery from failures. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Here, a correction code is a learned representation of corrective language, grounded spatial evidence, execution history, and an action proposal. MetaBrain supplies corrective supervision during training and grounded guidance during execution. The correction encoder and adapter learn to turn this guidance into actions, absorbing corrective knowledge into trainable action-policy weights. At deployment, fresh codes adjust behavior while all weights remain fixed. This couples learning from foundation models with using their reasoning when new failures arise. The underlying action model, A2-WLA, augments a vision-language-action policy with motion-aware history and a latent world model. Surprisingly, even before online correction, this simple architecture with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset, approximately 2.21×2.21\times the 2025 winner’s reported public score of 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On the full 100-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public set, the complete system combines MetaBrain, diagnostic agents, and learned correction to achieve 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% complete-task success. The same action design also supports short-horizon bimanual manipulation, achieving 93.98% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, or 95.05% with the complete system. Real-robot evaluation spans 12 tabletop tasks across five household settings, where A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success compared with 26.67% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation tests recovery during sustained execution. At two filter-handling steps, a history-conditioned Adapter raises post-failure completion from 14.00% to 94.00% and from 8.00% to 82.00%, relative to retries by A2-WLA without the Adapter. To support development at this scale, our training infrastructure reaches 427.1 samples per second, approximately 4.03×4.03\times the throughput of a π0.5\pi_{0.5} reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure as an efficient, usable framework for embodied learning.

Recent evaluations show that general-purpose models can generate robot actions without task-specific parameter updates. On the 42-task RoboDojo evaluation, GPT-6 Astra ranks above the 40 public policies included in the comparison, although precision and dynamic control remain limitations [1]. Specialized action models can benefit from this progress by absorbing foundation-model knowledge into their weights and consulting these models during execution. Learning recurring decisions into a compact policy offers efficient control, while access to a capable foundation model can help address unfamiliar failures. The challenge is to combine these routes to sustain coherent behavior throughout an activity.

A robot must do more than choose a plausible next action. Each interaction changes the conditions for what follows. A recovered grasp may secure an object in an orientation that prevents its later placement, and a successful local correction may leave the original goal unfinished. Long-horizon autonomy therefore requires reasoning about both the immediate physical state and the consequences of changing it. This motivates our focus on how learned control, task reasoning, and diagnostic evidence cooperate across complete activities, including failures and the attempts to recover from them.

Recovery exposes the need to connect task reasoning directly to action generation. Language-guided skill selection and feedback-driven replanning help a robot decide what to attempt next [2, 3, 4]. After a failed grasp, however, choosing to retry does not determine how the next attempt should differ. The controller must adjust its approach, target alignment, or gripper timing using evidence from the failed interaction. Language-conditioned robot policies and vision-language-action (VLA) models learn to map observations and instructions to control [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Predictive approaches, from GR-1 to world-action models (WAMs), also connect action generation with future visual dynamics [11, 12, 13]. The interface must make newly inferred corrections usable within this control process. Spatial planning, joint reasoning-and-action models, and learned recovery offer ways to connect decisions to execution [14, 15, 16]. We focus on a learned interface that carries corrective intent together with its spatial and temporal evidence into the action policy, so that a diagnosis can change the next trajectory while preserving the task goal.

We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework that coordinates reasoning, diagnostic grounding, and continuous control through a shared execution record. Its action model, A2-WLA, learns from long-horizon demonstrations and uses recent visual history and predicted scene features to generate actions. A vision-language coordinator, MetaBrain, maintains the task goal and examines unexpected outcomes. Diagnostic agents provide perceptual, spatiotemporal, and interaction evidence, using object localization, segmentation, tracking, available depth, and robot-state signals. These are complementary diagnostic functions rather than a fixed list of mandatory perception models. MetaBrain combines their findings with executed action history to formulate a correction. The action policy then attempts the correction, and the observed result becomes evidence for the next decision.

Our central principle is code as a scaling interface. The code is a learned conditioning representation that brings together a recovery instruction, grounded spatial evidence, executed history, and a fresh action proposal. Language expresses the intended change, while the other inputs specify the physical situation in which it must be made. A residual adapter uses the resulting code to modify the action expert’s hidden states throughout trajectory generation. This gives heterogeneous agents a common route for influencing continuous control without requiring them to share an architecture. During training, MetaBrain-generated instructions and expert continuations teach the correction encoder and adapter how corrective reasoning should change actions. This absorbs corrective knowledge into trainable action-policy parameters while leaving the A2-WLA backbone frozen. During deployment, new guidance changes the code and the generated behavior, with all parameters fixed. The framework therefore links knowledge learned into the policy with reasoning supplied when execution needs it.

A strong action model is the starting point for this cooperation. A2-WLA augments a vision-language-action policy with motion-aware history and a latent world model that predicts future visual features. Surprisingly, this simple architecture, together with action pretraining and task specialization, already yields strong long-horizon performance before adding online correction. On the 50-task public subset of BEHAVIOR 2026, one shared A2-WLA model reaches 0.4522 Q-score, and task-specialized policies reach 0.5755. The latter is approximately 2.21×2.21\times RLC’s public score of 0.2605 in the 2025 competition [17]. RLC, the 2025 winner, combines learned control with explicit stage-transition logic, a gripper-reopening heuristic, and a radio-specific rollback rule [18]. The strong result from our comparatively simple action architecture highlights how much competence can be learned within the policy before adding agent-guided intervention.

We then ask what grounded intervention adds to that competence. Across all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 tasks, the multi-model A2-WLA baseline obtains 0.6040 Q-score and 40.60% complete-task success. Adding MetaBrain, diagnostic evidence and learned correction raises these public-set results to 0.6411 and 45.40%, with at least one successful episode on 88 tasks. Fixed-policy Adapter ablations and a disjoint set of task instances test the correction mechanism separately from model selection.

We also test the action model beyond long-horizon whole-body control. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success across Clean and Randomized conditions, and the complete system reaches 95.05%. Real-robot experiments span 12 tabletop tasks across five household settings, with 20 trials per task and configuration. Without high-level correction, the full A2-WLA recipe reaches 57.92% macro success, compared with 26.67% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} [9]. These tasks cover storage, retrieval, food preparation, pushing and tool use. Long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation takes approximately four minutes per run. At two filter-handling steps, a lightweight history-conditioned Adapter completes 94/100 and 82/100 post-failure trials, compared with 14/100 and 8/100 for retries by the same frozen A2-WLA policy with the Adapter disabled. These real-robot recovery tests complement the full correction-interface experiments in simulation.

Long-horizon experiments also make iteration expensive. We therefore develop training and evaluation infrastructure alongside the models. Our implementation processes 427.1 demonstration samples per second on eight GPUs, approximately 4.03×4.03\times the throughput of a π0.5\pi_{0.5} reference implementation on the same hardware. The reference uses matching image resolution and action horizon, with each implementation’s batch size chosen for resource utilization. For evaluation, ideal linear scaling of the estimated 1,275-hour serial runtime gives a naive eight-GPU baseline of approximately 159.4 hours. Our eight-Pro6000 simulation and policy worker pool completes the 1,000-episode suite in 18.1 hours, approximately 8.8×8.8\times faster than this projected baseline, with the reasoning service hosted separately.

We will progressively release the system code, models, training scripts and optimized infrastructure at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/A2MEAS. The release is intended to give researchers and developers an efficient, usable framework for training, evaluating and deploying embodied agents across large-scale simulation platforms and real-world tasks.

Our contributions are threefold. ♠\spadesuit We introduce A2-MEAS and its code interface, which learns from MetaBrain-generated corrective supervision and connects online reasoning and grounded evidence to continuous control with deployment-time parameters fixed. ♠\spadesuit We establish the performance of the simple A2-WLA architecture across long-horizon BEHAVIOR and short-horizon RoboTwin evaluations, and test physical manipulation across diverse tabletop tasks and long-horizon coffee preparation. The complete system reaches 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% success on the BEHAVIOR 2026 public set. ♠\spadesuit We provide infrastructure with a 4.03×4.03\times training-throughput gain under the stated hardware conditions and an evaluation speedup of approximately 8.8×8.8\times relative to the estimated naive eight-GPU baseline, making full-suite testing practical within a daily research cycle.

1 The A2-MEAS framework

General embodied intelligence requires a system to connect its intentions to the physical consequences of its actions. Over a long activity, a robot must remember what remains to be done while responding to changes in objects, contacts, and its own configuration. A successful movement is useful only if the resulting state supports continued progress. A2-MEAS addresses this problem by coupling learned action generation with task-level reasoning and evidence-based diagnosis.

The framework contains three cooperating groups of agents (Figure 1). A2-WLA generates continuous actions from the task instruction and observed history. MetaBrain monitors execution in relation to the full goal and determines when the next attempt should change. Diagnostic agents investigate the physical questions needed to make that decision. All three use a shared record of actions and observations. When execution requires intervention, a learned correction interface converts their instruction and evidence into changes inside the action generator.

Section 1.1 explains how the shared record coordinates these agents. Section 1.2 introduces the action model, its observation and prediction components, and the adapter that accepts corrective guidance. Section 1.3 follows a recovery example from diagnosis through corrected execution. Sections 2 and 3 then develop the interface and action model in detail.

1.1 Framework architecture and coordination

A2-MEAS couples a local control loop with a task-level reasoning loop. The local loop repeatedly generates action chunks from the task instruction and recent observations. The task-level loop uses the resulting evidence to decide whether execution can continue, whether the goal has been achieved, or whether recovery is needed. A shared execution record stores the goal, dispatched controls, and observed outcomes. It gives all agents a common account of what has actually happened without requiring them to share a backbone or run at the same frequency.

The execution layer dispatches only a prefix of each predicted chunk, then obtains fresh observations before the next policy call. Thus, control is closed-loop across chunks even though an uninterrupted prefix executes without a new policy prediction. A2-WLA handles ordinary changes through this repeated observation–action cycle. When monitoring detects an abnormal outcome, the runtime pauses pending controls and asks MetaBrain to review the evidence. Verified recovery returns execution to the nominal loop, and verified completion ends the episode.

Diagnostic agents are invoked when a decision depends on an unresolved physical condition. Table 1 groups their functions into perceptual grounding, spatiotemporal grounding, and interaction assessment. Perception locates objects and regions. Temporal analysis tracks how they move relative to one another. Interaction assessment combines those observations with available robot-state, contact, and geometric evidence. For example, seeing an object between the gripper fingers does not establish a secure grasp. Tracking whether it moves with the hand, together with gripper-state evidence, supports a more informative assessment. Depth or reconstructed geometry can supply additional evidence when available. Each finding retains its observation source and timestamp so that MetaBrain can distinguish a supported conclusion from a missing observation.

The result determines what happens next. Evidence that supports the required condition permits execution to continue. Evidence of a mismatch prompts a correction. Insufficient evidence prompts another observation within the sensing budget. A negative answer and an unknown answer therefore lead to different decisions. Conditional tool invocation keeps ordinary control inexpensive while allowing several diagnostic capabilities to contribute when a correction needs them.

1.2 Action model and correction interface

Let gg denote the complete task instruction, retained throughout nominal execution. We index the physical control step at which the policy executes by tt. The policy input xtx_{t} aggregates synchronized multiview visual observations, a finite temporal window of past visual frames, and the current proprioceptive state sts_{t} comprising joint positions and end-effector configurations.

A2-WLA combines three sources of action context. A vision-language backbone encodes the task instruction and visual observations. Its motion-aware history encoder represents changes across recent frames. A latent world model predicts future visual features from a transition representation inferred by the backbone. The action expert uses current context, predicted future context, and proprioception to generate controls. Future observations supervise training but are unavailable at deployment. Section 3 describes these components and the three stages used to train the base policy.

During standard nominal operation, A2-WLA executes with the correction branch deactivated. We designate this default configuration as the base policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, parameterized by θ\theta. At invocation step tt, with sampling randomness suppressed in the notation, it jointly predicts a multi-step continuous action chunk and an auxiliary local-phase progress estimate

(A^t,p^t)=πθ​(xt,g),A^t∈ℝH×da,p^t∈[0,1]H,(\hat{A}_{t},\hat{p}_{t})=\pi_{\theta}(x_{t},g),\qquad\hat{A}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}},\quad\hat{p}_{t}\in[0,1]^{H}, (1)

where HH is the prediction horizon and dad_{a} is the number of values in each robot control command. Row a^t,j∈ℝda\hat{a}_{t,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} proposes the control for step t+jt+j, with j∈{0,…,H−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,H-1\}. The corresponding entry p^t,j\hat{p}_{t,j} estimates relative progress within the annotated local-phase interval. Its training target follows position within a demonstrated skill phase, from values near zero at the beginning to one at the final annotated step. This estimate supports execution monitoring, while observed physical outcomes determine whether to continue execution, request correction, or confirm task completion.

The correction branch adds a second way to influence action generation. Its condition encoder combines a recovery instruction, verified spatial evidence, relevant executed history, and an uncorrected proposal from the base policy. The resulting code conditions a residual adapter inside the action expert. The code is computed once per generated chunk, while the adapter recomputes its hidden-state adjustment at each flow-integration step. Later action layers turn the modified representation into a corrected trajectory. This mechanism supplements the policy’s ordinary visual and predictive context without updating its weights (Section 2).

The robot executes only an initial prefix of the generated chunk. Let LtL_{t} be the number of controls actually dispatched at call tt, with 1≤Lt≤Hexec≤H1\leq L_{t}\leq H_{\mathrm{exec}}\leq H whenever execution starts. The BEHAVIOR reference configuration predicts H=50H=50 controls, executes at most Hexec=32H_{\mathrm{exec}}=32, and uses da=23d_{a}=23 control dimensions. After an uninterrupted prefix, the next observation is acquired at t+32t+32, and a new prediction replaces the unused 18 controls. If monitoring interrupts the prefix, the next observation corresponds to t+Ltt+L_{t}. A candidate rejected before dispatch produces no executed controls and is not logged as an action prefix.

The execution record RtR_{t} stores the history available at physical step tt. Each entry links observations before and after a dispatched prefix to its actual controls, executed length, and timestamps. Camera identifiers, coordinate frames, task identifiers, and available local-phase annotations preserve the meaning of those records. Unexecuted proposals are stored separately. The short visual window in xtx_{t} serves immediate action prediction, whereas RtR_{t} supplies a longer history for diagnosis and recovery.

After a dispatched prefix finishes or is interrupted at step t+Ltt+L_{t}, the runtime returns a feedback bundle bt+Ltb_{t+L_{t}} containing the updated execution records, diagnostic findings, progress estimates, and status. The status is RUNNING during nominal execution, TASK_COMPLETE after completion checks succeed, or ABNORMAL when execution requires review. Progress predictions describe the proposed chunk and are interpreted together with the executed controls and observed outcomes. MetaBrain uses this feedback to decide what evidence or corrective instruction is needed next.

1.3 From failure diagnosis to corrected action

The correction interface becomes useful when observing the changed scene is not enough to change an ineffective behavior. Figure 2 illustrates a filter-placement example. The support ring should rest on the cup rim, with the filter hanging inside the opening. If one edge slips below the rim, continuing downward may wedge the ring or disturb the cup. Recovery instead calls for lifting the ring, aligning it above the opening, and lowering it again.

After detecting an anomaly, the framework pauses pending controls and establishes a recovery state. MetaBrain examines the observations and executed controls between the last verified nominal state and the detected deviation. It asks the diagnostic agents to assess contact stability and the spatial conditions required for another placement attempt. Perceptual tools identify the filter and cup regions, while temporal tracking helps bound the interval in which support was lost. Available robot-state and contact evidence informs the recovery assessment. Geometric and kinematic checks assess whether the proposed lifting motion is feasible. The recovery instruction is finalized once its required premises have been resolved. If occlusion leaves a necessary condition unknown, the system requests another observation within its sensing budget. The instruction specifies the adjustment and reference frame, while A2-WLA generates the continuous trajectory.

At the recovery state, the base policy first generates an uncorrected proposal. This proposal shows what the policy would attempt without intervention. The condition encoder combines it with the instruction, spatial evidence, and executed history. In the filter example, “realign the filter” is therefore interpreted in relation to a particular ring orientation, cup opening, and attempted movement. The adapter can then apply different residuals to different action positions, allowing a chunk to lift first and approach again later. These are learned adjustments rather than a prescribed geometric trajectory.

Before dispatch, the runtime checks that the evidence remains current and that the candidate satisfies the available joint-limit and obstacle-clearance checks. It executes a prefix, records the outcome, and checks whether the support condition has been restored. Successful recovery returns the robot to the unfinished task. Otherwise, the new observations and failed attempt inform another recovery pass. The reference configuration allows at most three physical retries and 60 seconds per anomaly, with separate sensing and reasoning limits specified in Section 2.6.

The methodological contribution is code as a scaling interface, a learned connection between grounded recovery context and the action policy’s internal representation. MetaBrain can express what should change, diagnostic tools can establish where and under what conditions, and the action model can translate that context into movement. During training, the condition encoder and adapter learn from MetaBrain-generated guidance, offline-mined candidate deviations, and expert continuations while the original A2-WLA checkpoint remains frozen (Section 2.5). At deployment, fresh guidance and evidence change the correction code, which shapes action generation with all model parameters fixed. The interface thus connects corrective knowledge learned during training with the physical context encountered during execution.

2 Cooperation through grounded correction codes

A diagnosis is useful to a robot only if it changes what the robot does next. Our organizing principle, code as a scaling interface, makes the connection through a learned representation that carries reasoning and diagnostic evidence into action generation. MetaBrain describes the intended adjustment, diagnostic agents ground it in the observed scene, and the execution record identifies what has already been tried. A condition encoder combines this context with the current action proposal into a correction code. The adapter uses the code inside A2-WLA to shape the next movement. Language is one input to this interface, together with the spatial and temporal evidence needed to make the instruction actionable. Different agents can contribute through the same context schema while retaining their own architectures.

2.1 MetaBrain diagnosis and recovery instructions

MetaBrain formulates a recovery instruction utu_{t} from the task goal gg and feedback btb_{t}, including relevant executed history and diagnostic findings. The public-set system uses Qwen3.8-27B [19] for this role, separately from the 2B vision-language backbone inside A2-WLA. It compares the observed outcome with the intended operation and requests further evidence when a condition is unresolved. The instruction describes how the next attempt should change while preserving the original goal. The memory-limited hidden-set deployment uses a smaller coordinator, as described in Section 5.2.3.

A visible failure may occur several controls after the action that caused it. An unstable grasp, for example, may become apparent only when the object slips during transport. MetaBrain therefore examines the interval from the last verified nominal state to the detected anomaly, including the controls actually executed. This history helps distinguish errors during approach, grasp closure, and transport. When utu_{t} requests a spatial adjustment, it also identifies the reference frame, such as the camera, robot base, or object. MetaBrain specifies the intended change, while A2-WLA determines the continuous controls.

2.2 Diagnostic agents and evidence verification

Before a recovery instruction is executed, the framework checks the physical conditions on which it depends. The diagnostic functions summarized in Table 1 contribute complementary evidence. For grasp assessment, perception identifies the target, temporal tracking measures its motion relative to the hand, and available proprioceptive signals describe the gripper state. Together, these observations help assess whether the object moves consistently with the gripper. If the evidence is insufficient to answer the query, the result remains unknown.

A request planner routes each question to tools that can supply the necessary evidence. DINO-based features support visual matching, while SAM-based segmentation supplies object masks [20, 21]. Tracking, depth or 3D estimation, robot-state readings, and analytical kinematics provide additional evidence when available. These tools support the diagnostic functions in Table 1. They are selected according to the query and sensor configuration, and their outputs retain the source image, timestamp, and coordinate frame.

The interface supports six kinds of questions. (i) State and attribute queries assess visible properties. (ii) Spatial queries assess relative positions and region membership. (iii) Interaction queries assess grasp, contact, or support. (iv) Temporal queries identify changes such as release or slippage. (v) Instance queries track identity and detect objects that have appeared or disappeared. (vi) Feasibility queries assess reachability and clearance under the available geometry and robot model. Multiple query types can use the same tool, and a query can use multiple tools.

Verification distinguishes a negative answer from insufficient evidence. An observed obstacle calls for a different path, while an occluded region may require another view. All conditions required by an instruction must be supported before that instruction is dispatched. Geometric evidence must also be internally consistent. A point and mask must refer to the same view and frame, or be transformed into a common coordinate system, and the selected interaction point must lie in the intended region. Available robot-model checks assess reachability, joint limits, and obstacle clearance. Ordinary deployment uses observations and robot-state readings, without ground-truth object poses or privileged simulator segmentation. The simulator-assisted scheduling controls in Section 6.4.2 are a separate diagnostic experiment.

2.3 Correction context and code construction

An instruction such as “realign toward the opening” leaves several questions unanswered. The policy must know which opening is intended, where it is in the current observation, and what the previous attempt did. The CorrectionContext in Table 2 keeps the instruction, spatial evidence, executed history, and uncorrected proposal in separate fields. Each field retains enough provenance to associate it with the correct recovery state.

MetaBrain supplies the instruction after reviewing diagnostic findings. Grounding agents attach object regions, interaction points, and spatial relations. The runtime supplies executed controls and their observed outcomes. Feasibility assessments inform both instruction construction and the decision to dispatch a candidate. This division lets different tools contribute through a common schema while preserving the distinction between an observation, an inferred relation, and a proposed action.

The recovery text and its referenced offset direction jointly form utu_{t}. The failure window selects and links relevant executed records in RtR_{t}, while verified spatial evidence is encoded as GtG_{t}. These fields form the four code inputs. The task instruction gg enters the ordinary language-conditioning path. The input_features field references observation features and action hidden states used by the policy and adapter. These runtime references are distinct from the four inputs encoded into the fixed correction code.

After recovery preparation, the runtime acquires fresh observations at step tt. With correction disabled, A2-WLA generates the unexecuted proposal A^tbase\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{base}}. Let GtG_{t} encode the verified spatial evidence and let RtR_{t} supply the relevant executed history. The condition encoder combines these inputs with utu_{t} to produce a latent correction representation

ct=Eϕ​(ut,Gt,Rt,A^tbase),c_{t}=E_{\phi}(u_{t},G_{t},R_{t},\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{base}}), (2)

where ϕ\phi denotes all trainable correction-branch parameters, including the encoder, adapter, and residual scale below. The code ctc_{t} is a continuous learned representation of the correction context. It stays fixed while one corrected chunk is generated. The same verbal instruction can therefore produce different corrections when the evidence, history, or base proposal changes. Current visual features and predicted future context still enter through the policy’s ordinary conditioning paths.

2.4 Correction adapter for action generation

The action expert generates a chunk by integrating a learned flow field. Physical time is indexed by tt, while τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] indexes the internal noise-to-action process. For one policy call, let hτ∈ℝH×dhh_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{h}} be the action hidden states after layer nine, with hidden width dhd_{h}. We suppress the fixed physical index tt on these states. The residual adapter applies

hτ′=hτ+α⊙Cϕ​(hτ,ct),h^{\prime}_{\tau}=h_{\tau}+\alpha\odot C_{\phi}(h_{\tau},c_{t}), (3)

where α∈ℝdh\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} is a learned channel scale, broadcast over the HH action positions, and ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The code ctc_{t} is fixed for the chunk, but hτh_{\tau} and the adapter output are recomputed at every integration step. The remaining nine transformer layers predict the corrected flow velocity (Figure 3). The residual acts in hidden-feature space rather than directly specifying a joint-space offset.

Because the adapter reads each action position’s hidden state, its adjustment can vary across the chunk. A change in approach direction need not impose the same offset on later transport actions. The adapter’s output projection is initialized to zero and α\alpha to 0.10.1, so the initial residual is zero and the base network output is unchanged. The adapter uses a bottleneck width of 256. The complete correction branch, including the condition encoder, has fewer than 100M trainable parameters.

The task of turning on a radio (BEHAVIOR Task 000), shown in Figure 4, illustrates how this adapter translates a recovery instruction into a local motion adjustment. To activate the radio, the gripper must align with the small power button and then press toward the front panel. MetaBrain expresses this adjustment in language. Combined with spatial evidence, executed history, and a fresh base-policy proposal, the instruction is encoded as ctc_{t} (Equation (2)) and guides residual modulation of the action hidden states (Equation (3)). The remaining action layers turn the modified representation into continuous controls while the base model parameters remain fixed.

In the upper branch, the orange trajectory shows the adapter-guided adjustment. Base-policy execution then resumes in teal and completes the task. The lower branch shows a separate A2-WLA-only rollout in which the gripper approaches beside the button. These examples illustrate the division of work between MetaBrain’s recovery instruction, adapter-guided motion, and subsequent base-policy execution.

2.5 Correction data and adapter training

We construct correction supervision offline from the demonstration corpus (Figure 5). At a recorded state, the frozen base policy proposes an action chunk, which is compared with the expert continuation from that same state. Large deviations at critical manipulation steps provide candidate correction examples. These are unexecuted policy deviations, not observed physical failures. They teach the adapter how to change a proposal toward an expert continuation, while leaving a distribution gap to the failed execution states encountered at deployment.

Data mining focuses on skill transitions, pre-contact approach phases, and gripper actuation boundaries. At each sampled start tt, the frozen base policy receives the task prompt, robot state, current images, and causal observation history. It generates one uncorrected candidate chunk using the standard inference procedure, including the configured flow-integration steps. Future observations and expert continuations do not enter this candidate generation.

To quantify divergence between the policy’s proposal and the expert demonstration, both trajectories are mapped into an identical coordinate frame, kinematic unit system, and temporal indexing convention. A 32-step comparison window defines the directional residual and normalized error

Δ​at,j=at,j−a^t,jbase,et=maxj∈Jt⁡d⁡(a^t,jbase,at,j),\Delta a_{t,j}=a_{t,j}-\hat{a}_{t,j}^{\mathrm{base}},\qquad e_{t}=\max_{j\in J_{t}}d(\hat{a}_{t,j}^{\mathrm{base}},a_{t,j}), (4)

where at,ja_{t,j} is the expert action at local index jj in the segment starting at tt, and a^t,jbase\hat{a}_{t,j}^{\mathrm{base}} is the corresponding base-policy prediction. The set JtJ_{t} contains positions within the 32-step comparison window that are both valid and marked as critical manipulation steps. Positions beyond a skill boundary or demonstration termination are excluded. The distance d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) normalizes differences using the configured scale of each action component. A window is retained when ete_{t} exceeds the threshold δ\delta. Windows without a valid critical position are skipped. Small perturbations of the sampled start around critical events provide coverage of approach and timing variations.

The annotation pipeline uses open-vocabulary object localization, SAM-based masks, and MetaBrain to construct corrective instructions. The candidate-to-expert deviation indicates the required change, while recorded images locate the relevant objects and regions. The annotation prompt includes the task, local phase, deviation, and grounded entities with their camera and frame identifiers. Unresolved spatial fields remain null. Expert actions and future frames can inform offline labels, but they are not supplied to the base-policy proposal. The correction text describes the intended change and its reference frame, while the expert continuation supervises its metric realization.

Training and deployment use the same context schema with different evidence sources. Online, failure_window identifies an observed execution anomaly. Offline, it marks the interval where an unexecuted proposal deviates from the demonstration. The historical fields contain only the demonstrated prefix before tt, and the proposal is stored separately in inferred_action_chunk. This separation prevents an unexecuted candidate or a future target from being treated as experienced history.

Each sample retains its trajectory identifier, timestamps, and base-checkpoint metadata. Overlapping windows are consolidated when measuring dataset duration. Mining makes one candidate-generation call at each sampled start, and previously mined samples can be reused or refreshed for another checkpoint. Retained supervision is capped at 2% of the 1,950-hour corpus, or 39 hours, with priority given to critical steps that have complete spatial evidence. Schema checks and sampled manual inspection assess whether annotations agree with the images and trajectory deviations. Training freezes the base parameters θ\theta and updates only the correction parameters ϕ\phi against the expert continuation.

Correction training minimizes the masked flow-matching objective in Equation (14), with ctc_{t} supplied as an additional condition. The base parameters θ\theta remain frozen, and only the correction-branch parameters ϕ\phi are updated. Expert continuations provide the action targets, using the same validity masks and flow-time convention as base-policy training. In this way, MetaBrain’s corrective knowledge enters action-policy learning through its generated instructions, and the encoder and adapter learn the mapping from that guidance to physical action. The knowledge is absorbed into the correction parameters ϕ\phi, while the pretrained action parameters θ\theta remain unchanged. This is supervision of a learned correction interface, not direct distillation of MetaBrain’s internal representations. The mining offset Δ​at,j\Delta a_{t,j} is defined in control space, whereas the adapter predicts hidden-state residuals. The flow objective learns how those residuals should change the generated actions.

Correction training uses eight GPUs, BF16 precision, and a global batch size of 256. AdamW uses β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 0.01, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. Training runs for 6,000 steps, with a 1,000-step linear warm-up to 10−410^{-4} followed by cosine decay toward 10−510^{-5}. Validation and checkpoint saving occur every 400 steps. Each evaluated adapter is paired with its corresponding base checkpoint.

2.6 Closed-loop runtime orchestration

Figure 6 summarizes the recovery loop. After detecting an anomaly, the runtime pauses pending controls and saves the observations, robot state, and executed history. Recovery preparation may include controlled stopping, posture adjustment, or contact release when required. The runtime then reacquires observations and robot state. Returning the robot to an earlier pose does not imply that the object or environment has been restored. MetaBrain and the required diagnostic agents use this updated evidence to prepare the recovery instruction. Spatial evidence, the relevant observation history, the base proposal, and the corrected candidate must all correspond to the current recovery state. Before dispatch, the runtime checks evidence freshness, joint limits, and obstacle clearance. If the state changes during candidate generation, it refreshes the affected evidence and regenerates the candidate before execution.

After each corrective prefix, the runtime checks whether the required physical condition has been restored. If so, nominal execution resumes. Otherwise, the failed attempt and updated observations inform another recovery query. Each anomaly allows at most two additional viewpoints, each with a five-second allowance, and three physical retries. A MetaBrain request times out after ten seconds, and the entire recovery event is limited to 60 seconds. Resubmitting a query does not reset these counters. The runtime aborts recovery when a required condition cannot be verified or an applicable budget is exhausted.

MetaBrain determines how the intended operation should change, grounding agents assess the physical conditions needed for that change, and A2-WLA generates the continuous controls. This division of labor allows reasoning and diagnostic capabilities to contribute through the shared CorrectionContext. New tools can be incorporated when their outputs preserve the field semantics, coordinate conventions, and representations expected by the correction encoder.

3 The A2-WLA action model

A2-WLA supplies the continuous control capability on which grounded correction operates. It combines a 2B-parameter Qwen3-VL backbone [22], a multiview latent world model, and an approximately 300M-parameter Gemma-style action expert with 18 transformer layers (Figure 7). The backbone interprets the task and visual history. The world model predicts future scene features. The action expert uses both current and predicted context, together with proprioception, to generate continuous controls. The history encoder, world model, and action expert are described first, followed by data construction and training. The architecture is shared across embodiments through a masked action representation, while camera inputs, state fields, and control semantics follow each robot’s configuration.

The base policy is trained in three stages. World-model pretraining learns from multiview transitions. Vision-language pretraining adds action and embodied-language supervision. Joint optimization then trains the continuous policy and its auxiliary objectives. Correction learning is a separate fourth stage that freezes the base policy and trains the interface described in Section 2.5.

3.1 Motion-aware visual history encoding

A single image often leaves an interaction ambiguous. An object between the gripper fingers may be securely held, slipping, or still resting on a surface. The history encoder supplies temporal evidence before visual tokens enter the language backbone. Each camera contributes five past frames and the current frame, arranged chronologically. A temporal patch kernel of size two groups them into three frame pairs. The first four visual blocks process the pairs with shared parameters.

Each paired representation is compressed with adaptive 4×44\times 4 pooling and learned queries. Let fkf_{k} denote the compressed representation of pair k∈{0,1,2}k\in\{0,1,2\}. Adjacent differences provide temporal features

dk=LN⁡(W⁡(fk+1−fk)+PE⁡(k)),k∈{0,1},d_{k}=\operatorname{LN}\bigl(W(f_{k+1}-f_{k})+\operatorname{PE}(k)\bigr),\qquad k\in\{0,1\}, (5)

where WW is a learned projection, PE⁡(k)\operatorname{PE}(k) is a learned interval-position embedding, and LN\operatorname{LN} denotes layer normalization. These features supply keys and values for gated cross-attention in later visual blocks. Residual fusion, the remaining visual blocks, and token merging produce the sequence passed to the language backbone. This design combines appearance with changes across the sampled observation window.

The history representation is recomputed from the sliding window at each policy call, without recurrent hidden-state accumulation. Its feature differences encode observed change rather than calibrated velocity, because the sampled frame intervals can vary. The longer execution record RtR_{t} remains separate and is used for diagnosis. Section 3.4.1 specifies frame sampling and camera alignment.

3.2 Multiview latent world model

Visual history describes recent changes, while the world model predicts the scene features relevant to the next action. The head camera captures workspace layout, and wrist cameras provide local views of the gripper and nearby objects. Occlusion and camera motion can make a transition ambiguous in any single view. Building on latent-action modeling in LaWAM [13] and Wave-0 [23], we train a shared latent variable to explain changes across these complementary views. The representation is learned from visual transitions and is not tied to a fixed joint-vector dimensionality.

The world model contains a frozen visual encoder, an inverse model, and a future-feature predictor. For clarity, we suppress the physical step index tt within this subsection. Let F=(F1,…,FV)F=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{V}) be the current patch features from VV camera views, and let F+F^{+} contain features observed 50 control steps later. During world-model pretraining, the inverse encoder EinvE_{\mathrm{inv}} produces a shared transition latent z∗z^{*}. The predictor then reconstructs future features for each view

z∗=Einv​(F,F+),F^v+=Dv​(F,z∗).z^{*}=E_{\mathrm{inv}}(F,F^{+}),\qquad\hat{F}_{v}^{+}=D_{v}(F,z^{*}). (6)

Reconstructing all views from a shared latent variable encourages consistency across their predicted changes. This joint constraint can help resolve ambiguity in individual views.

At deployment, future frames are unavailable. Learned queries in the vision-language backbone instead predict a latent z^\hat{z} from current and historical observations and the task instruction. The backbone also supplies current-context tokens CC. The future predictor uses z^\hat{z}, and a spatial compressor PP aggregates its outputs into future-context tokens

F^v+=Dv​(F,z^),C+=P⁡(F^+),\hat{F}_{v}^{+}=D_{v}(F,\hat{z}),\qquad C^{+}=P(\hat{F}^{+}), (7)

where F^+=(F^1+,…,F^V+)\hat{F}^{+}=(\hat{F}_{1}^{+},\ldots,\hat{F}_{V}^{+}). Camera embeddings preserve view identity, and validity masks exclude missing views. We write C+∈ℝNfut×dcC^{+}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{fut}}\times d_{c}}, where NfutN_{\mathrm{fut}} is the total number of compressed tokens across views and dcd_{c} is their context width. Attention projections map these tokens to the action expert’s hidden width dhd_{h}.

3.3 Action expert with correction adapter

The action expert receives current-context tokens CC, future-context tokens C+C^{+}, and a projection of the proprioceptive state sts_{t}. Its 18 transformer layers alternate between the two context streams. With zero-based indexing, even layers cross-attend to CC and odd layers cross-attend to C+C^{+}. Every layer also applies self-attention among the action tokens. This gives both observed and predicted scene information repeated opportunities to influence the generated trajectory.

An embodiment-specific input/output mapping handles each robot’s state fields and control semantics. For shared tensor processing, an action chunk with dad_{a} active control dimensions is padded to width dmaxd_{\max}. A validity mask excludes padded dimensions and invalid timesteps from losses and dispatch. In the learning equations below, AA and A^\hat{A} denote these normalized, padded chunks. At execution, the output mapping removes padding and restores native units. This keeps the learning representation distinct from the physical control interface in Equation (1).

The action expert uses conditional flow matching [24]. For one policy call, we omit the fixed physical index tt and write the noisy chunk as AτA^{\tau}. The velocity network vθ(Aτ,τ∣s,C,C+)v_{\theta}(A^{\tau},\tau\mid s,C,C^{+}) is conditioned on the current state s=sts=s_{t} and both context streams. Inference starts from Gaussian noise at τ=1\tau=1 and integrates toward τ=0\tau=0 in ten numerical steps. The integration rule is deterministic conditional on the initial noise, while the sampled noise makes the policy stochastic. Physical execution time and internal flow time are separate. Section 3.4 defines the path and target velocity.

Condition tokens remain fixed during numerical integration, so their projected keys and values are computed once and cached across flow steps. The noisy action tokens and velocity estimates are updated at each step. During recovery, the continuous correction code ctc_{t} conditions a residual adapter after the ninth transformer layer, corresponding to zero-based index 8. The adapter adds α⊙Cϕ​(hτ,ct)\alpha\odot C_{\phi}(h_{\tau},c_{t}) to the action hidden states, and the remaining nine layers predict the corrected flow velocity. The code stays fixed for one candidate, while the hidden states and residual are recomputed at every integration step. All policy and correction-branch parameters remain fixed during deployment.

A separate head predicts local-phase progress at each action position. The BEHAVIOR reference configuration predicts 50 controls and executes at most 32 before requesting a new chunk. Longer predictions provide context for the dispatched prefix, and the next observation allows the policy to revise the remaining movement. Predicted progress helps monitoring but does not establish physical completion. A detected abnormal outcome invokes the recovery interface.

3.4 Training details

3.4.1 Training sample construction

Each training sample is anchored at one physical step. It contains the task instruction, robot state, synchronized multiview history, and a target action chunk. Recorded future frames and phase annotations provide additional targets when available. Input histories end at the anchor step. Future observations and actions appear only as supervised targets or offline annotation evidence.

For the BEHAVIOR 2026 configuration described here, training uses the official corpus of 20,000 teleoperated demonstrations, totaling approximately 1,950 hours across 100 household tasks and seven scenes [25]. Demonstrations are collected through the JoyLo whole-body interface, which coordinates the mobile base, torso, arms, and grippers. The average trajectory lasts 5.86 minutes, and the annotations cover 31 skill primitives, including grasping, pouring, wiping, and articulated-object manipulation [26]. These extended trajectories require the policy to handle object-state changes and dependencies between successive operations.

Recorded timestamps align multiview images, proprioceptive states, and robot controls. Task instructions and skill intervals supply the corresponding language and phase annotations. Official head-camera streams recorded at 720×720720\times 720 resolution and dual wrist-camera streams recorded at 480×480480\times 480 resolution are bilinearly downsampled to 224×224224\times 224 for policy training, matched with continuous robot states and controls at 30 Hz. Self-supervised world model pretraining ingests visual inputs at 256×256256\times 256 spatial resolution. Robot states and action dimensions use quantile normalization computed from the training split. The embodiment adapter instantiates 23-dimensional absolute continuous commands encompassing whole-body actuation channels.

Training windows retain the complete task instruction, while skill annotations define the temporal boundaries used for auxiliary progress supervision and transition sampling. When skill intervals overlap, the earlier-starting skill determines the phase label. Action supervision continues across skill boundaries wherever trajectory steps are valid. Separate masks identify valid phase labels, progress targets, and control dimensions, so a missing auxiliary label does not discard otherwise valid action supervision.

History sampling schedule.

Each training input contains five past frames and the current frame. We sample one positive look-back offset from each of the five intervals bounded by [30,84,138,192,246,300][30,84,138,192,246,300], using a log-uniform distribution within each interval. The frame at offset Δ\Delta is taken from t−Δt-\Delta. We append the frame at tt and sort the six frames chronologically, using the same timestamps across cameras. Deployment uses fixed relative offsets [−256,−205,−154,−60,−30,0][-256,-205,-154,-60,-30,0]. At 30 Hz, training look-back offsets span one to ten seconds, and the oldest deployment frame is 8.53 seconds old. A lookup before episode start repeats the initial frame and carries a temporal-padding flag.

Transition sampling and regularization.

The boundary-sampling configuration increases sample weights fivefold within 60 frames on either side of a primitive transition. Proprioceptive dropout decreases linearly from 0.3 to 0.05 over the first 60% of training. This encourages the policy to use visual context rather than rely only on robot state. Non-gripper action errors receive velocity-dependent weights in [0.5,1.5][0.5,1.5], giving more emphasis to faster demonstrated movements. These weights are distinct from the binary validity masks. Optional pace conditioning appends a quantized demonstration-duration category to the task text. At inference, the category comes from a checkpoint-specific task mapping or an explicit request, not the unknown duration of the ongoing episode.

3.4.2 World-model and vision-language pretraining

The first two stages learn representations before continuous-policy optimization. Stage 1 trains the world model from multiview transitions. Stage 2 trains the vision-language backbone with latent-action targets, FAST action tokens, continuous action candidates, and embodied question answering.

We denote losses by LL and stop-gradient by sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot). The operators MSEM\operatorname{MSE}_{M} and MAEM\operatorname{MAE}_{M} average squared and absolute error over entries enabled by mask MM. Masks refer to the domain of each loss. They may select valid action dimensions, timesteps, camera views, or annotations. A loss with no valid target entries is omitted.

World-model pretraining.

Stage 1 trains the inverse model and future-feature predictor while keeping the visual encoder frozen. Let mv∈{0,1}m_{v}\in\{0,1\} indicate a valid current–future pair for camera view vv, and let wv>0w_{v}>0 be its reconstruction weight. Using the transition latent z∗z^{*}, we minimize

Lworld=∑v=1Vwv​mv​SmoothL1⁡(F^v+,Fv+)∑v=1Vwv​mv+λreg​Reg⁡(z∗),L_{\mathrm{world}}=\frac{\sum_{v=1}^{V}w_{v}m_{v}\,\operatorname{SmoothL1}(\hat{F}_{v}^{+},F_{v}^{+})}{\sum_{v=1}^{V}w_{v}m_{v}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\operatorname{Reg}(z^{*}), (8)

where SmoothL1\operatorname{SmoothL1} compares predicted and observed feature tensors, Reg\operatorname{Reg} denotes latent regularization, and λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}} controls its weight. Samples without a valid current–future view pair are excluded. After Stage 1, the inverse encoder is frozen to provide latent-action targets. The future predictor is transferred to the policy and updated again during joint continuous-action training.

Shared vision-language supervision.

Stage 2 trains the vision-language backbone and its prediction heads with four complementary objectives

Lpre=LFAST+λAQ​LAQ+λLA​LLA+λVQA​LVQA.L_{\mathrm{pre}}=L_{\mathrm{FAST}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{AQ}}L_{\mathrm{AQ}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{LA}}L_{\mathrm{LA}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{VQA}}L_{\mathrm{VQA}}. (9)

Each loss is evaluated only for samples with the corresponding targets. The shared backbone processes visual context and task language, while output queries and heads supply the different predictions. The following paragraphs define each supervision stream. During teacher-forced language or action-token training, causal masking prevents a prediction from seeing later target tokens. Policy-conditioning queries must likewise remain independent of answer and action targets.

▶\blacktriangleright Latent-action prediction. A latent-action head maps learned query tokens to a predicted transition vector z^\hat{z}. It learns from the frozen inverse model through

LLA=‖z^−sg⁡(z∗)‖22.L_{\mathrm{LA}}=\|\hat{z}-\operatorname{sg}(z^{*})\|_{2}^{2}. (10)

The frozen teacher uses current and future observations to produce the target z∗z^{*}. The student predicts z^\hat{z} from current and past observations and language. Stop-gradient keeps the teacher fixed while the student learns to predict its transition representation. Future observations are therefore used for supervision, not as deployed policy inputs.

▶\blacktriangleright Discrete actions with FAST. The FAST frequency-domain tokenizer [27] converts an action chunk AA into discrete tokens y1,…,yTy_{1},\ldots,y_{T}. Predicting this sequence teaches the backbone to represent action trajectories. Training uses teacher-forced cross-entropy

LFAST=−∑r=1Tlogpθ(yr∣x,g,y<r),L_{\mathrm{FAST}}=-\sum_{r=1}^{T}\log p_{\theta}(y_{r}\mid x,g,y_{<r}), (11)

where TT is the token-sequence length, pθp_{\theta} is the conditional distribution over the discrete vocabulary, and y<ry_{<r} is the target token prefix. The FAST configuration uses a vocabulary of 2,048 tokens and a sequence budget of 256 tokens. FAST supplies action-sequence supervision to the backbone, while the flow-matching action expert generates continuous controls at deployment.

▶\blacktriangleright Continuous candidates and scores. Parallel action queries predict NN continuous trajectory candidates A^(n)\hat{A}^{(n)} and their scalar errors e^n\hat{e}_{n}. For candidate nn, the supervised error is en=MAEM⁡(A^(n),A)e_{n}=\operatorname{MAE}_{M}(\hat{A}^{(n)},A), with mask MM excluding inactive control dimensions and padded steps. We train the closest candidate against the demonstrated chunk and train the error head against detached candidate errors

n∗=arg⁡minn⁡en,LAQ=en∗+λscoreN​∑n=1N(e^n−sg⁡(en))2.n^{*}=\arg\min_{n}e_{n},\qquad L_{\mathrm{AQ}}=e_{n^{*}}+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{score}}}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\hat{e}_{n}-\operatorname{sg}(e_{n}))^{2}. (12)

Selecting one winning candidate for the entire horizon encourages distinct trajectory hypotheses rather than requiring every candidate to approximate the same demonstrated path. Detaching the target error ene_{n} prevents the score-regression loss from updating trajectory predictions through that target. Gradients through the predicted score e^n\hat{e}_{n} can still update the score head and any shared representations on its branch.

▶\blacktriangleright Embodied question answering and local goals. Stage 2 also trains the backbone to answer questions about scene layout, task progress, and the next local goal. Inputs contain multiview frames, the task instruction, and a question. Demonstration-derived answers describe milestones such as repositioning an object or orienting it toward a receptacle. These goals use the standard language-output head. Target answers enter only the teacher-forced answer sequence and remain hidden from policy-conditioning queries.

3.4.3 Joint policy optimization

Stage 3 jointly trains the VLM backbone, future predictor, action expert, and enabled auxiliary heads. Flow matching supplies the main continuous-action objective. Action-query supervision continues on samples with valid trajectories, and auxiliary losses constrain predicted features, action representations, geometry, and task information. FAST token prediction is disabled during this stage.

▶\blacktriangleright Conditional flow matching. The continuous action expert models whole-body trajectories by learning a time-dependent velocity field along a probability path connecting pure Gaussian noise to demonstration segments. For a demonstrated trajectory AA, we construct the intermediate noisy segment

Aτ=(1−τ)​A+τ​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I),A^{\tau}=(1-\tau)A+\tau\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), (13)

where τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] denotes continuous flow time and II represents the identity covariance. This linear interpolation between demonstration actions and Gaussian noise has target velocity ϵ−A\epsilon-A. The action expert network vθv_{\theta} is supervised to regress this velocity conditioned on the noisy segment, proprioceptive state ss, causal context embeddings CC, and predicted prospective visual features C+C^{+} through

LFM=𝔼τ,ϵ,A[MSEM(vθ(Aτ,τ∣s,C,C+),ϵ−A)].L_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\epsilon,A}\left[\operatorname{MSE}_{M}\bigl(v_{\theta}(A^{\tau},\tau\mid s,C,C^{+}),\,\epsilon-A\bigr)\right]. (14)

The expectation uses demonstrated action chunks, standard Gaussian noise, and uniformly sampled τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]. The mask MM excludes padded steps and inactive control dimensions. Since the target is the derivative with respect to increasing τ\tau, inference integrates the learned field with negative time increments from one to zero. This matches the noise-to-action convention in Section 3.3.

▶\blacktriangleright Prospective feature consistency. To retain predictive visual information during supervised policy updates, joint optimization aligns causal world predictions with observed future features through

Lfuture=∑v=1Vmv​‖F^v+−Fv+‖F2∑v=1Vmv,L_{\mathrm{future}}=\frac{\sum_{v=1}^{V}m_{v}\|\hat{F}_{v}^{+}-F_{v}^{+}\|_{F}^{2}}{\sum_{v=1}^{V}m_{v}}, (15)

where the squared Frobenius norm sums feature errors within a view. Here mv=1m_{v}=1 requires a valid current–future feature pair, and samples without one are excluded. This equation expresses the feature-consistency objective at a conceptual level. The training recipe records separate distillation and perceptual components for this purpose, as distinguished below.

▶\blacktriangleright Action-chunk representation alignment. We pool the action expert’s tokens over the prediction horizon, project them, and normalize the resulting vector to obtain z^a\hat{z}_{a}. A fixed linear projection of the flattened target chunk, followed by the same normalization, produces zaz_{a}. The alignment objective is

Lalign=MSE⁡(z^a,sg⁡(za)).L_{\mathrm{align}}=\operatorname{MSE}(\hat{z}_{a},\operatorname{sg}(z_{a})). (16)

The target zaz_{a} summarizes the current sample’s complete action chunk, rather than the chunk from a later policy call. It is used only for supervision and is not supplied to the deployed policy. The objective encourages chunk-level representation consistency, while flow matching determines the individual control values.

▶\blacktriangleright End-effector geometry. Joint-space errors can have different Cartesian consequences across poses. We therefore compare predicted and target end-effector motion through a common whole-body kinematic mapping KrK_{r}. Let A^\hat{A} denote the predicted clean action chunk supplied to this auxiliary objective. Both chunks are converted to the same physical units and evaluated from the same initial state ss

Lr=MSEMr⁡(Kr​(s,A^),Kr​(s,A)),r∈{pos,rot},L_{r}=\operatorname{MSE}_{M_{r}}\bigl(K_{r}(s,\hat{A}),K_{r}(s,A)\bigr),\qquad r\in\{\mathrm{pos},\mathrm{rot}\}, (17)

where rr selects position or rotation increments of the active end-effectors. The mask MrM_{r} selects valid end-effectors, timesteps, and geometric components. Both branches use the same reference frame and rotation convention. These losses encourage agreement with demonstrated motion. They do not test collision avoidance, contact stability, or dynamic feasibility.

▶\blacktriangleright Semantic identity and temporal progress. For samples with a valid task identifier, an auxiliary classification head averages the final-layer action representations and predicts task identity through cross-entropy Ltask=−log⁡ptask​(ytask)L_{\mathrm{task}}=-\log p_{\mathrm{task}}(y_{\mathrm{task}}), where ytasky_{\mathrm{task}} is the task label. This objective preserves task information in the action features without replacing the language instruction. It is separate from the local-phase and progress objectives grouped in LstatusL_{\mathrm{status}}.

A separate linear head with sigmoid activation predicts relative skill-phase progress p^t,j\hat{p}_{t,j} at each action position. For the annotated skill phase [t0,t1)[t_{0},t_{1}) active at the anchor step tt, the target is the fraction of the interval elapsed after the corresponding action step

pt,j=clip⁡(t+j−t0+1t1−t0,0,1).p_{t,j}=\operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{t+j-t_{0}+1}{t_{1}-t_{0}},0,1\right). (18)

Only positions satisfying t0≤t+j<t1t_{0}\leq t+j<t_{1} contribute to the masked mean squared progress loss. Progress masks are defined separately from action-validity masks. The status objective LstatusL_{\mathrm{status}} aggregates the enabled local-phase and progress objectives and excludes the task-identity loss LtaskL_{\mathrm{task}}.

Progress is learned from relative positions within demonstrated skill phases and is not a probability of physical completion. The predicted curve describes a proposed action chunk, including its unexecuted suffix. Feedback to MetaBrain refers to the observed local phase and is interpreted together with the executed prefix and observed outcomes. Whole-episode progress is not substituted for skill-phase progress. A value near one does not independently establish physical completion, which requires verification of the physical completion conditions.

The total training objective combines these terms

Ltrain=\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{train}}={} LFM+Lprior+λAQ​LAQ+Laux+0.1​(Ldistill+Lperc),\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{FM}}+L_{\mathrm{prior}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{AQ}}L_{\mathrm{AQ}}+L_{\mathrm{aux}}+0.1(L_{\mathrm{distill}}+L_{\mathrm{perc}}), (19)
Laux=\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{aux}}={} Ltask+Lstatus+Lalign+5×10−6​Lpos+10−3​Lrot,\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{task}}+L_{\mathrm{status}}+L_{\mathrm{align}}+5\times 10^{-6}L_{\mathrm{pos}}+10^{-3}L_{\mathrm{rot}},

where LdistillL_{\mathrm{distill}} and LpercL_{\mathrm{perc}} implement the future-feature consistency objective in Equation (15). The conceptual LfutureL_{\mathrm{future}} is not added again. The Gaussian-prior loss LpriorL_{\mathrm{prior}}, task-identity loss LtaskL_{\mathrm{task}}, and aggregate status loss LstatusL_{\mathrm{status}} each enter the total objective with unit weight. End-effector position and rotation losses have weights 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} and 10−310^{-3}, respectively. Each objective is evaluated only where its required observations and labels are valid.

Following the idea of knowledge insulation [28], we attenuate gradients through the current-context token path from the VLM to the action expert. For a representation hh on this path, we apply

KI⁡(h)=γ​h+(1−γ)​sg⁡(h).\operatorname{KI}(h)=\gamma h+(1-\gamma)\operatorname{sg}(h). (20)

This operator preserves the forward activation and scales gradients on this path by γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1]. We apply it to current-context tokens supplied to the action expert. It does not freeze the VLM or scale every gradient entering it. Future-context prediction and auxiliary supervision remain separate paths through the training graph.

3.4.4 Sampling schedules, optimization, and hyperparameters

The objectives above specify supervision. The following schedules specify how training data, flow evaluations, and parameter updates are allocated.

▶\blacktriangleright Data mixture and adaptive flow sampling. Training batches sample heterogeneous datasets according to configured mixture probabilities. For each demonstration ii, the action expert first evaluates N0=2N_{0}=2 noise-time pairs. Their masked flow losses provide a difficulty score

ri=Mean1≤r≤N0⁡(Li,r)+βsample​Std1≤r≤N0⁡(Li,r),r_{i}=\operatorname{Mean}_{1\leq r\leq N_{0}}(L_{i,r})+\beta_{\mathrm{sample}}\operatorname{Std}_{1\leq r\leq N_{0}}(L_{i,r}), (21)

where βsample\beta_{\mathrm{sample}} controls the contribution of loss variation. More difficult demonstrations receive additional flow evaluations, with at most eight pairs per demonstration and a target batch average of four.

To separate the sampling budget from each demonstration’s explicit loss weight, we average flow losses within each demonstration and then across the batch

Lbatch=1B​∑i=1B(1Ni​∑r=1NiLi,r),L_{\mathrm{batch}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\left(\frac{1}{N_{i}}\sum_{r=1}^{N_{i}}L_{i,r}\right), (22)

where BB is the batch size, Ni∈{2,…,8}N_{i}\in\{2,\ldots,8\} is the number of flow evaluations for demonstration ii, and Li,rL_{i,r} is its masked flow loss at sample rr. This reduction gives every demonstration the same explicit outer weight while assigning more computation to difficult examples. The multimodal backbone runs once per demonstration, and its representations are shared across flow branches. Backbone objectives independent of flow time are evaluated once. Auxiliary objectives that depend on action-suffix states use one designated branch, so their effective weights do not grow with NiN_{i}.

▶\blacktriangleright Optimization schedules. Table 3 summarizes the three base-model stages. Each uses 64 GPUs. The world-model checkpoint transferred to later stages is taken at step 45,000. The final 1% of recorded sequence intervals forms an internal validation partition for monitoring world-model training, separate from the downstream benchmark evaluation.

Optimizer dynamics are specialized according to layer types across training phases. Stage 1 applies the AdamW optimizer with hyperparameter settings β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), numerical stabilization constant ϵopt=10−8\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}=10^{-8}, and unit gradient accumulation, excluding normalization gains and linear biases from weight decay regularization. Stage 2 combines FAST and VQA cross-entropy, continuous action-query regression, and latent-action distillation. The continuous action expert is not evaluated in this stage. During Stage 3 continuous-action training, structured weight matrices within attention projections and feed-forward layers are optimized via Local Muon, while remaining embedding and auxiliary layers are updated via AdamW. Muon configurations maintain a momentum factor of 0.95, Nesterov momentum acceleration, and five internal Newton–Schulz orthogonalization iterations.

▶\blacktriangleright Loss weights. Stage 2 uses λAQ=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{AQ}}=1.0, λLA=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{LA}}=0.1, and λVQA=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{VQA}}=1.0. Stage 3 reduces the action-query weight to λAQ=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{AQ}}=0.1 and uses knowledge-insulation scale γ=0.1\gamma=0.1 on the current-context path. Task and status supervision follow Equation (19). The phase-classification component has an implementation default of 0.1 and must be explicitly configured for the reported status-supervision recipe.

4 Infrastructure for Efficient Training and Deployment

Long-horizon embodied learning is limited by the cost of collecting, processing, and evaluating extended interaction sequences. For A2-WLA, multiview history encoding and repeated flow evaluations make training expensive. In BEHAVIOR, simulation, rendering, policy inference, and variable episode lengths also make full-suite evaluation costly. Our infrastructure addresses these costs through efficient data access, shared model computation, distributed optimization, and parallel simulation scheduling.

We report training and evaluation comparisons separately. Training comparisons measure demonstration throughput under the stated hardware and batch configurations. For evaluation, we compare the measured optimized worker pool with a naive eight-GPU baseline projected from recorded unoptimized serial-worker costs. The projection normalizes the GPU count by assuming ideal linear parallelism, while preserving the reference per-worker cost.

4.1 Training Optimization and Distributed Scaling

▶\blacktriangleright I/O and Data Ingestion. Continuous action optimization via flow matching constitutes the primary computational bottleneck within the multi-stage training pipeline. In the baseline single-device implementation, each optimization step requires approximately 3.03 seconds, with input processing alone accounting for 1.30 seconds. This delay stems from redundant visual decoding, where identical temporal video frames are repeatedly decompressed across overlapping observation windows. To eliminate this bottleneck, we consolidate frame extraction through batch JPEG decompression, map demonstration datasets into Apache Arrow shared-memory caches, and streamline inter-dataset indexing. These adjustments reduce per-step input preparation time from 1.30 seconds to 28 milliseconds. Together with asynchronous background data prefetching, single-GPU step latency drops to 1.13 seconds, representing a 2.7×2.7\times training acceleration. Furthermore, expanding dataset diversity from ten to 100 manipulation tasks incurs only a 3% throughput penalty, confirming that data routing scales with task coverage without introducing proportional preprocessing overhead. Figure 8 summarizes separate measurements of data preparation, step latency, throughput, and startup time.

▶\blacktriangleright Distributed Startup and Synchronization. Distributed training across multi-GPU clusters frequently suffers from slow initial startup and hidden communication stalls. During job initialization, dozens of worker processes often attempt to parse the same raw dataset files simultaneously, causing severe storage contention and prolonged idle waiting. We parallelize dataset preparation, share sampler weights from rank zero, and delay parameter initialization on non-primary ranks to reduce repeated loading. During active training steps, device synchronization is further streamlined by locking the backward communication order into a fixed static schedule. This configuration groups scattered parameter gradients into contiguous memory buffers for unified all-reduce synchronization, while eliminating redundant broadcast transfers for static model buffers that do not change during training.

▶\blacktriangleright Prefix Computation Sharing. A substantial computational redundancy in continuous flow matching arises from sampling multiple noise-time pairs (τ,ϵ)(\tau,\epsilon) for each demonstration trajectory. Although these stochastic pairs evaluate distinct flow targets, they share identical visual histories, language instructions, and proprioceptive states. Rather than evaluating the complete model repeatedly, our implementation computes the multimodal prefix once through the vision-language backbone. The resulting representations are shared across the action expert’s noise-time evaluations, which are batched instead of run serially. The reference configuration uses four evaluations per demonstration on average, while the adaptive schedule varies the number by sample. Each flow sample processes its own noisy continuous action and time coordinate, whereas resulting backpropagation gradients accumulate into the shared prefix representation. For the same samples and masks, shared-prefix execution preserves the per-demonstration reduction in Equation (22). Gradients from the action branches accumulate into the shared prefix. This equivalence concerns the shared-prefix computation and does not establish equivalence across complete training trajectories. Together, shared-prefix execution and Arrow caching achieve 261.9 samples per second on eight GPUs.

▶\blacktriangleright Kernel Stabilization and Optimizer Sharding. Additional latency in deep transformer training arises from dynamic sequence lengths and kernel launch overhead. We mitigate these delays by caching static tokenizer outputs, rotary position embeddings, and task metadata whenever input sequences permit reuse. Stable sequence-length buckets and padding upper bounds that increase only when necessary reduce repeated Triton compilation and autotuning. These optimizations reduce static host-side overhead from 33 milliseconds to 0.8 milliseconds and forward latency from 243.7 to 210.7 milliseconds. At the optimization boundary, we coordinate AdamW with the matrix-oriented Local Muon optimizer. We distribute 126 independent matrix updates across eight local ranks according to their computational cost. Each update uses the configured Newton–Schulz iterations, and the results are gathered in BF16. Sharded Local Muon reduces optimizer latency from 67.0 to 19.7 milliseconds. Bitwise equivalence was verified for the compared sharded optimizer updates.

The final SDPA-based implementation reaches 427.1 demonstration samples per second on eight GPUs with global batch size 256. Multiple flow samples from one demonstration count as one demonstration sample. The π0.5\pi_{0.5} reference reaches 106 demonstration samples per second on the same GPU hardware with matching image resolution and action horizon. Each implementation uses a batch size chosen to utilize the available resources. The resulting 4.03×4.03\times ratio compares implementation throughput under these conditions. At 64 Pro6000 GPUs, the reported scaling efficiency is approximately 98% relative to ideal linear scaling for the tested configuration. Figure 9 illustrates the aforementioned optimization gains.

4.2 Heterogeneous Model Serving and Robot Execution

The reported BEHAVIOR deployment separates high-level reasoning from action generation. The Qwen3.8-27B model used by MetaBrain runs in BF16 with tensor parallelism across two GPUs. The complete A2-WLA policy, including its 2B vision-language backbone, world-model components, action expert, and correction adapter, runs in BF16 on a separate GPU. Base and corrected action generation both use ten flow-integration steps.

The simulator and policy service communicate through synchronous WebSocket requests. After executing up to 32 controls from a 50-step chunk, the runtime acquires fresh observations and requests the next chunk. At 30 Hz, an uninterrupted 32-step prefix spans approximately 1.07 seconds. The policy-call interval also includes inference and communication time. Observation buffers and execution records are cleared at each episode boundary to prevent information from carrying over between episodes.

4.3 Scalable Simulation Infrastructure for Long-Horizon Benchmarks

The complete BEHAVIOR 2026 evaluation comprises 100 tasks with ten evaluation instances per task, yielding 1,000 episodes across the benchmark’s seven scenes. The measured run contains 15,113,902 simulator control steps. At 30 Hz, this is approximately 140 hours of simulated manipulation, averaging 8.40 minutes per episode. This rollout duration differs from the 5.86-minute mean of the training demonstrations reported in Section 3.4.1. Photorealistic rendering, rigid-body contact dynamics, and neural network inference add substantial computational work to these trajectories. Recorded unoptimized single-worker costs give an estimated serial runtime of 1,275 hours for the suite. We define a naive eight-GPU baseline by running one unchanged worker per GPU and distributing episodes evenly. Assuming ideal linear scaling gives 1,275/8=159.3751{,}275/8=159.375 hours, reported as 159.4 hours, or approximately 6.27 episodes per hour (Table 4). This projection assumes unchanged per-worker performance, balanced workloads, and no added startup, scheduling, communication, or shared-service contention. Actual episode lengths vary, so our scheduler allows workers to take on new instances as they finish their current tasks.

Our evaluation infrastructure combines cache reuse, faster simulator startup, and coordinated CPU and GPU resource allocation. These changes reduce repeated work in the evaluation pipeline while keeping task definitions, simulation settings, and model execution logic unchanged. The optimized configuration supports three concurrent workers per Pro6000 GPU, including simulation and policy inference. On an eight-GPU node, this arrangement sustains 24 active simulation workers in parallel. A dynamic scheduler assigns the next task to each available worker, reducing idle time between unequal-length episodes.

The optimized evaluation node completes the 1,000 episodes in 18.1 hours, corresponding to approximately 55.2 episodes per hour and an aggregate throughput of 7.7×7.7\times simulated real time. The eight-GPU allocation in Table 4 describes the simulation and policy workers. The separately hosted reasoning service is described in Section 4.2, so this node allocation should not be read as the total hardware requirement of every full-system deployment.
