Relative to the projected naive eight-GPU runtime, the measured reduction is (1,275/8)/18.1≈8.8×(1{,}275/8)/18.1\approx 8.8\times. This comparison includes cache reuse, startup optimization, dynamic scheduling, and the increase from one to three workers per GPU. It removes the direct one-versus-eight GPU-count difference, but remains conditional on the reference per-worker performance and ideal-scaling assumptions. A measured baseline on the same GPU model and model-serving configuration is still needed to isolate these contributions experimentally. The distributed scheduler further supports multi-node deployment, supporting up to 96 concurrent simulator workers across a four-machine cluster. This infrastructure makes a complete evaluation practical within a day under the measured configuration, supporting more frequent model and system comparisons.

5 Experimental Evaluation

We evaluate A2-MEAS across long-horizon household activities, bimanual manipulation, and physical robot tasks. The experiments examine how model specialization and agent coordination affect task completion, whether the learned action policy transfers across scene variations, and how the complete system executes sequential manipulation in the real world.

5.1 Experimental Setup

BEHAVIOR 2026 evaluates long-horizon whole-body control over 100 household tasks spanning multiple scenes. The official dataset contains 20,000 human demonstrations with a mean duration of 5.86 minutes (351.54 seconds) [26]. The distribution has a long tail, with some demonstrations lasting much longer than the mean (Figure 10). Our public-set analysis uses records selected from evaluation batches, with ten instances per task and 1,000 episodes per configuration. The single-model baseline uses one A2-WLA checkpoint across all tasks. The multi-model baseline selects an action model and execution configuration for each task. Building on this action capability, A2-MEAS coordinates MetaBrain, grounding agents, and A2-WLA through learned correction codes that connect task reasoning and spatial evidence to continuous action generation. Official hidden-set results are reported separately in Section 5.2.3.

The reference action interface uses six frames per view, 23-dimensional actions, and a 50-step prediction horizon, with the first 32 steps executed before the next observation. Integration steps and executed prefixes follow the corresponding configuration. All model parameters remain fixed at test time, and human takeover, timeouts, and exhausted episode budgets count as failures.

We report task-macro Q-score, complete-task success rate (SR), and successful task coverage. Q-score measures the fraction of goal conditions satisfied, while SR requires completion of the entire task. Let QiQ_{i} and SiS_{i} denote the mean goal-satisfaction score and success fraction for task ii. Over KK tasks,

Q=1K​∑i=1KQi,SR=100K​∑i=1KSi.Q=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}Q_{i},\qquad\mathrm{SR}=\frac{100}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}S_{i}. (23)

Successful task coverage counts tasks with at least one complete success among their ten evaluation instances. Equal episode counts per task make task-macro and episode-micro success rates coincide in these benchmark evaluations.

5.2 Long-Horizon Household Manipulation on BEHAVIOR

5.2.1 Overall Performance

In our public-set evaluation records (Table 5), A2-MEAS obtains a Q-score of 0.6411 and a complete-task success rate of 45.40%, with 454 successes in 1,000 recorded episodes and at least one success on 88 tasks. The corresponding multi-model and single-model results achieve 0.6040 and 0.4597 Q-score, respectively. The recorded task coverage increases from 70 to 80 to 88 tasks across the three configurations, while the number of tasks with mean Q-score of at least 0.8 rises from 17 to 30 to 34. These patterns motivate the task-level analysis below.

5.2.2 Task-Level Performance and Completion Reliability

Figure 11 shows the performance of all 100 tasks in the public-set records. Eleven tasks are completed in every recorded instance, spanning activities such as turning on a radio, cooking hot dogs, installing a modem, and laying tile floors. At the other end of the distribution, eight tasks have Q-scores below 0.2, including pizza preparation and patio cleaning, both with zero goal satisfaction. This spread shows that broad benchmark coverage coexists with sharply concentrated weaknesses.

Performance varies substantially even within familiar activity families. Cooking hot dogs and making microwave popcorn both achieve 100.00% success, whereas cooking bacon reaches 20.00% and making pizza has no successful instances. Installation tasks exhibit a similar spread. Smoke-detector and modem installation succeed in all ten instances, while scanner installation succeeds in three of ten.

High goal satisfaction also does not guarantee reliable completion. Of the 34 tasks with Q-score at least 0.8, five have complete-task success rates of 40.00% or lower. Food storage is a pronounced example, with a Q-score of 0.8375 but only one successful instance out of ten. Moreover, ten of the twelve tasks with no complete successes still achieve positive Q-scores. Gift-basket assembly and boxing books for storage reach 0.6500 and 0.5500, respectively. These results expose a gap between satisfying a substantial subset of goal conditions and consistently satisfying the entire task specification.

The task-wise profile identifies two complementary targets for improvement. For tasks with substantial goal satisfaction but few complete successes, the target is reliable satisfaction of all required conditions within the same episode. For tasks with near-zero scores, the target is to establish effective execution of the activity itself. Reporting Q-score together with complete-success counts makes these distinct performance regimes visible and provides a concrete basis for selecting tasks for further model and system development.

5.2.3 Comparison with Public Results

Table 6 compares public-set results. Our public evaluation used a remotely hosted Qwen3.8-27B MetaBrain. For the official hidden-set submission, limited bandwidth between the organizers’ evaluation site and our server in China required a self-contained Docker deployment. The 24 GB GPU-memory limit forced us to replace the 27B coordinator with Qwen3.5-2B [39]. This substantial reduction in coordinator capacity limits the submitted system, so the hidden-set results do not fully represent the capability of the 27B-based system.

On the official hidden set, A2-MEAS obtains a verified Q-score of 0.4975 and 32.05% complete-task success [40], compared with 0.4951 and 30.95% for the separate A2-WLA submission. The 2B coordinator thus provides a small gain. In our tests, the 2B coordinator was less accurate than Qwen3.8-27B at deciding when to intervene and sometimes interrupted execution unnecessarily. The reported hidden-set results were obtained with the submitted Docker configuration using the 2B coordinator. We will release the Qwen3.8-27B version of MetaBrain for further evaluation and development.

Table 8 places our public-set results on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 subset alongside methods evaluated on the public dataset of BEHAVIOR 2025, including RLC, Comet, Openpi Comet, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and G0.5. The BEHAVIOR 2025 entries report public-dataset tests and are grouped by their reported evaluation settings. On task IDs 0–49, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6191 Q-score and 41.40% success across 500 recorded episodes.

5.3 Bimanual Manipulation on RoboTwin 2.0

RoboTwin 2.0 evaluates 50 bimanual tasks under Clean and Randomized settings [41]. The randomized scenes vary background, clutter, lighting, table height, and language. Table 8 summarizes public reference results alongside our configurations, which use A2-WLA as the action policy and add agent-guided correction in the complete system. The A2-WLA configuration completes 100 episodes per task in each setting, for 10,000 episodes in total. Public references retain the evaluation protocols reported by their respective sources. We report complete-task success for both settings, with Average defined as their arithmetic mean.

A2-WLA achieves 94.26% success in Clean scenes and 93.70% under randomization, averaging 93.98%. This is 14.23 percentage points above the reported π0.5\pi_{0.5} result of 79.75% and 0.73 percentage points above G0.5 at 93.25%. Agent coordination raises the average to 95.05%, a further 1.07-point gain, while MotuBrain reports 95.95% under its own protocol. Our simple A2-WLA architecture is thus competitive with leading bimanual policies without requiring a separate large-scale pretraining strategy tailored to this benchmark. At the same time, success rates near 95.00% leave limited room to distinguish systems on these short tasks. We include RoboTwin as a reference for local manipulation competence, while the longer BEHAVIOR and real-robot tasks more directly test sustained coordination and recovery.

5.4 Real-World Manipulation

5.4.1 Short-Horizon Tasks

We evaluate 12 tabletop tasks across five household settings, comprising the study, bedroom, living room, kitchen, and entryway. The tasks include storage and retrieval in confined spaces, pushing with obstacle avoidance, food preparation, and parcel handling, testing grasping, placement, action sequencing, and contact control under varied object sizes, spatial constraints, and contact conditions. We use π0.5\pi_{0.5} as the principal generalist baseline because of its strong manipulation performance across diverse real-world environments [9], and compare it with four fine-tuned A2-WLA configurations. For a fair real-robot comparison, high-level feedback and test-time correction are disabled.

Each task uses 200 training trajectories, and a separate policy is trained for each task and configuration for 60,000 steps from the specified initialization. The A2-WLA configurations include base fine-tuning, the multiview latent world model, a six-frame history window, and FAST action-token initialization (Table 10). For the full configuration, the vision-language backbone and motion-aware history encoder are initialized from weights jointly trained with FAST on 12 tasks for 60,000 steps, while the action expert is initialized from pretrained action-policy weights. The FAST classification loss is disabled during subsequent A2-WLA training. Sections 3 and 6.1 describe the model components and simulation ablations. These configurations use different complete training recipes. We evaluate each task and configuration over 20 trials and compute macro success as the arithmetic mean of the per-task success rates across all 12 tasks (Table 10).

Table 10 summarizes the policy configurations and their macro success rates across the 12 tasks. The full A2-WLA configuration achieves 57.92% macro success, compared with 39.58% for base fine-tuning and 26.67% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}. The full configuration exceeds base fine-tuning by 18.33 percentage points, computed from the underlying counts.

The per-task results in Table 10 show that the full configuration outperforms π0.5\pi_{0.5} on all 12 tasks, with gains spanning several types of manipulation. Food-waste sorting improves from 2/20 to 16/20 successful trials, keyboard pushback from 6/20 to 17/20, and bookshelf organization from 4/20 to 13/20. These tasks involve pouring, pushing around obstacles, and placing objects in confined spaces, respectively. The improvements therefore extend beyond object pickup to operations that require different action sequences and contact conditions. Figure 12 illustrates these execution sequences and compares the two policies on each task.

The gains are nevertheless uneven. The full configuration completes only 4/20 eye-drop/medicine retrieval-and-return trials, 5/20 parcel-unpacking trials, and 6/20 parcel-packing trials. Its result on medicine retrieval is also below the 5/20 of Configuration 3, so the aggregate improvement does not imply a gain on every task from every component. These remaining difficulties include small-object localization, retrieval in confined spaces, tool use, and ordered closure operations. Because these experiments disable high-level feedback and test-time correction, they measure the learned action policy’s ability to complete each task unaided. We next examine recovery during a longer coffee-preparation task.

5.4.2 Long-Horizon Pour-Over Coffee Preparation

Pour-over coffee preparation requires the robot to handle objects, position a filter, and complete a sequence of operations under changing contact and support conditions. In deployment, A2-MEAS completes the drink in approximately four minutes per run, with more than one hundred cups completed across deployment. To examine recovery within this longer activity, we evaluate two steps where a failed grasp can interrupt progress. Step 2 retrieves the filter from the rack and places it stably on the cup rim. Step 7 removes the filter from the cup and transfers it to a designated container.

For each step, we evaluate four experimental conditions with 100 trials per condition: direct base-policy execution, base-policy execution with the Adapter, base-policy retry, and Adapter recovery. The first two conditions start from the original task starting point, while the latter two start after a failed grasp and rollback. A trial succeeds when the robot completes the placement or transfer, releases the filter, and withdraws the gripper. Step 2 also requires stable support on the cup rim. Step 7 with a used filter requires removal of the grounds.

During recovery, the runtime pauses pending actions after an anomaly and updates the images and robot state. Using execution history and diagnostic evidence, MetaBrain proposes an adjustment, and A2-WLA generates corrective actions under Adapter modulation. After a short execution segment, the system observes the scene again and checks the recovery condition before deciding whether to continue. For a missed filter grasp, the correction aims to adjust the grasp position, regrasp, and lift the filter clear. Subsequent step completion measures whether execution can continue (Figure 13).

The real-robot experiments use a failure-history-conditioned Adapter. It takes current observations and up to 64 historical state transitions, reads the history through cross-attention, and adds a gated residual before the action output head. This variant conditions its residual on observations and failure history. The full interface in Figure 3 instead encodes all four CorrectionContext inputs and injects its residual at an intermediate action layer. The real-robot recovery results evaluate this history-conditioned Adapter. We freeze the base model and train approximately 860,000 Adapter parameters with a flow-matching objective, using measured state sequences from correction segments as supervision. The gate is initialized to zero, and all parameters remain fixed at deployment. After rollback, the Adapter completes Step 2 in 94/100 trials (94.00%) and Step 7 in 82/100 trials (82.00%), while base-policy retry succeeds in 14/100 (14.00%) and 8/100 (8.00%), respectively.

6 Ablation Studies and Long-Horizon Execution Analysis

We analyze how action-model design and grounded correction contribute to long-horizon manipulation, then compare full-task conditioning with subtask scheduling and examine whether local recovery leads to continued progress and task completion. To make repeated training and evaluation feasible, we use two 12-task subsets with different purposes. Selected12 covers object transport, storage, cleaning, cooking, and assembly, and supports the action-model and task-conditioning studies. A separate Adapter subset tests how corrective context changes execution, including button pressing in turning on a radio, object alignment in hanging pictures and attaching a camera to a tripod, and successive object-handling operations in bringing water and washing a baseball cap. These activities require control to account for target-relative position, object orientation, and the current manipulation stage, allowing us to examine the contributions of corrective language, spatial grounding, and execution history. Adapter comparisons keep the same action model frozen to hold its underlying control capability fixed, and a disjoint set of instances tests whether correction gains extend beyond the instances used in the ablations. Each evaluation round covers ten instances per task, or 120 episodes, and reports task-macro Q-score and complete-task success. The full 100-task system evaluation is reported separately in Section 5.

6.1 Base Action Model Ablations

Table 11 shows that the full A2-WLA achieves a Q-score of 0.5905 and a complete-task success rate of 50.28% on Selected12, exceeding the action-pretrained baseline by 0.1059 and 10.56 percentage points, respectively. All variants use a single policy without high-level correction or the correction Adapter.

▶\blacktriangleright Action Pretraining and Initialization. The pretraining stages in Section 3.4.2 introduce action supervision before continuous-policy optimization. We compare how much of this learned capability is transferred into the Selected12 policy. A six-frame model initialized from a general-purpose VLM reaches 0.2167 Q-score and 13.33% success. FAST initialization first teaches the backbone to predict discrete action tokens, raising these scores to 0.3453 and 20.83%. Action-policy initialization additionally transfers the action expert together with the vision-language backbone pretrained on all 100 tasks, reaching 0.4846 and 39.72% after downstream training. We therefore use action-policy initialization as the starting point for all subsequent cumulative ablations.

▶\blacktriangleright Temporal and Predictive Context. A2-WLA uses visual history to interpret recent interaction and a latent world model to anticipate scene changes (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). We first test whether the historical observations themselves help. With the same weights trained on six-frame inputs, replacing the current frame alone with the full history raises Q-score from 0.1582 to 0.2167 and success from 8.33% to 13.33%. This measures sensitivity to history removal at inference, including the change from the model’s six-frame training input. We then add predictive and motion representations to the action-pretrained baseline. Conditioning the action expert on predicted future features raises Q-score from 0.4846 to 0.5183 and success from 39.72% to 42.50% (A). Adding the motion-aware history encoder over the same six-frame window further improves these results to 0.5279 and 45.56% (B). Thus, retaining past observations and learning explicit representations of motion and future change provide complementary gains.

▶\blacktriangleright Training-Data Composition. The sampling design in Section 3.4.1 gives additional weight to skill transitions, where the policy must change its behavior as an operation ends. With the architecture and auxiliary objectives fixed, we jointly apply skill-boundary oversampling and primitive balancing. This raises Q-score from 0.5279 to 0.5546 and success from 45.56% to 46.67% (C), using the same trajectories and adaptive flow-sampling settings. We then broaden the training experience by perturbing initial robot and target-object positions within fixed training-scene layouts and retaining rollouts with terminal Q-score equal to one. Mixing these 2,400 successful trajectories, 200 per task, with the expert demonstrations brings the full model to 0.5905 Q-score and 50.28% success. The final comparison measures the combined effect of position perturbation, success filtering, and additional data. Together, the results show gains from both redistributing training toward skill transitions and expanding the successful execution examples. We next examine what task specialization reveals about the design of generalist action models.

6.2 Task Specialization and Model Design

A generalist action model must share knowledge across activities while retaining the control precision needed for specific interactions. In our development experiments, a model trained specifically on a 12-task subset outperformed the shared model trained on all 100 tasks when evaluated on that subset. This observation raises a model-design question about how to preserve the benefits of broad training without diluting the representations needed for particular scene layouts, object interactions, and action sequences.

We examine one form of specialization using a bank of A2-WLA policies trained on task subsets. Prior evaluations determine the task-to-model mapping and execution configuration, both fixed before the reported evaluation. Each episode uses one selected policy conditioned on the complete task instruction. Across all 100 tasks, this configuration reaches 0.6040 Q-score and 40.60% success, compared with 0.4597 and 27.20% for the shared model (Section 5). The gains combine specialization, checkpoint selection, and execution configuration.

These results motivate architectures that combine shared representations with specialized control capacity. One direction is to share the visual, temporal, and world-model backbone while allowing smaller action experts to adapt to different interaction patterns. A learned router conditioned on observations and task language could choose the appropriate action expert without a fixed mapping from benchmark task IDs. Another direction is to distill the specialized policies into one model, retaining their complementary skills while simplifying deployment. These possibilities remain to be tested under matched parameter and compute budgets. Grounded correction is complementary to this architectural question, and the following experiments isolate its contribution by keeping A2-WLA fixed.

6.3 Grounded Action Correction

The correction experiments use the 12-task Adapter evaluation subset described above and keep the A2-WLA weights fixed. The first ten instances per task form the condition-ablation set, and the last ten form a disjoint generalization set, each containing 120 episodes. Missing episode results contribute zero Q-score and count as failures. We first examine the information supplied to the Adapter, then compare correction interfaces and test additional instances.

6.3.1 Contribution of Correction Conditions

The condition encoder combines correction language utu_{t}, spatial evidence GtG_{t}, executed history RtR_{t}, and the current base proposal A^tbase\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{base}} into ctc_{t} (Equation (2)). We remove these inputs to evaluate their contribution while retaining the same action model and upstream reasoning modules. The language–grounding variant removes correction language, task text, and structured grounding together. It is therefore a joint semantic ablation rather than an isolated test of the recovery instruction. The history variant retains only the latest state–action record. Table 12 reports the resulting task performance.

The full Adapter achieves 0.6108 Q-score and 52.50% success, improving over the no-Adapter baseline by 0.0798 and 10.83 percentage points. Joint removal of language and grounding reduces performance to 0.5344 and 43.33%. Restricting history to one record yields 0.5356 and 44.17%. Both ablations bring performance close to the base policy, supporting the contribution of semantic–spatial context and extended execution history in this evaluation.

Removing the base candidate lowers Q-score by 0.0566 and success by 5.00 percentage points. Removing structured grounding lowers them by 0.0538 and 3.33 percentage points. Every tested deletion reduces performance relative to the complete condition set. The candidate anchors the adjustment to the action currently proposed by the policy, while grounding locates the correction in the physical scene.

6.3.2 Comparison of Correction Interfaces

We compare instruction restatement, end-effector geometric correction, and the latent residual Adapter on the 12-task Adapter evaluation subset (Table 13). Each interface uses high-level advice, spatial evidence, executed history, and a fresh base proposal. Trainable correction components use the same correction examples and source-trajectory split. These comparisons evaluate different intervention mechanisms; the interfaces are not matched for parameter count or computational cost. Physical recovery measures whether the required physical condition is re-established. Effective continuation additionally requires the next predefined meaningful task advance within a fixed window, while final completion records whether the original task goal is achieved within the remaining episode budget. For each method, the three recovery rates use episodes with at least one correction trigger, counting each episode once from its first trigger and including cases where no correction is executed. Q-score uses all 120 evaluation episodes. Triggered-episode cohorts can differ across interfaces. Effective continuation is measured within a fixed window, whereas final completion uses the remaining episode budget, so final completion need not be lower than the time-limited continuation rate.

Compared with VLM+IK, the Adapter achieves a higher physical recovery rate, 54.93% versus 52.05%, and a slightly higher Q-score, 0.6108 versus 0.6083. Its final completion rate among triggered episodes is 43.66%, compared with 45.21% for VLM+IK. These rates describe different triggered-episode cohorts, so they are not paired comparisons on identical failure states. VLM+IK applies geometric corrections through inverse kinematics, whereas the Adapter injects a correction code into the action expert’s hidden states during trajectory generation. Conditioned on the recovery instruction, scene evidence, execution history, and base proposal, the Adapter can coordinate the adjustment with the policy’s learned whole-body behavior across the action chunk. The observed improvement in physical recovery therefore does not translate into higher final task completion in this comparison.

The condition ablations vary the evidence supplied to one Adapter, whereas the interface comparison varies how the same corrective evidence changes behavior. The execution cases in Section 6.5 illustrate the distinction between local recovery and completing the original task.

6.3.3 Instance Generalization and Execution Cases

On the disjoint set of ten additional instances per task, the full Adapter reaches 0.6782 Q-score and 58.33% success, compared with 0.6185 and 50.83% for the base policy (Figure 14). The gains of 0.0597 and 7.50 percentage points correspond to nine additional completed episodes, increasing the success count from 61 to 70. The improvement therefore holds on both disjoint instance sets of the 12 correction tasks.

The correction-language ablation retains task text and structured grounding but removes corrective instructions and direction. It obtains 0.6336 Q-score and 52.50% success, below the full Adapter by 0.0446 and 5.83 percentage points. These results support the contribution of correction language alongside spatial evidence and history on additional instances of the same tasks.

Figure 15 relates the quantitative gains to hanging pictures, bringing water, and washing a baseball cap. Each column uses the same task instance and base-action checkpoint, with ten flow-integration steps and six input frames. Blue trajectories show A2-WLA-only motion, and orange trajectories show Adapter-controlled intervals. The outcome insets show subsequent observations and terminal task completion. In hanging pictures, the base rollout drops the frame after approaching the wall, while the Adapter-enabled rollout completes hanging. In bringing water, the correction occurs during bottle acquisition and is followed by task completion. In cap washing, repeated baseline grasp attempts end in a dropped cap, whereas the corrected rollout finishes the task. Across these examples, local alignment and object acquisition form the link between corrective intervention and continued execution.

We next compare execution with explicit subtask prompts and different scheduling strategies.

6.4 Full-Task Conditioning and Subtask Scheduling

6.4.1 Full-Task Conditioning versus Focus

Table 14 compares two training-and-execution configurations on Selected12. Both use the same pretrained initialization and demonstrations from the same 12 tasks. The baseline row is the first round of the action-pretrained configuration in Table 11, whose reported result averages three rounds. The single-round value here therefore differs from that three-round mean. The baseline uses the complete task instruction. Focus retains that goal and adds a Current focus: instruction selected by an asynchronous VLM.

On Selected12, the baseline achieves a task-macro Q-score of 0.5417 and a complete-task success rate of 45.83%, while Focus reaches 0.4411 and 30.83%, respectively. The corresponding differences are 0.1006 Q-score and 15.00 percentage points in favor of the baseline. As shown in Figure 16, this aggregate gap masks variation across tasks. Focus improves Q-score on three tasks, decreases it on seven, and ties on two. The largest gain is 0.1000 on making microwave popcorn, whereas the largest declines are 0.5333 on bringing water, 0.3000 on hanging pictures, and 0.2000 on cooking hot dogs. The task-specific gains therefore do not translate into an overall improvement for this Focus configuration.

The comparison evaluates the two training-and-execution configurations as a whole. To examine scheduling itself, the following control fixes the action model across all modes.

6.4.2 Scheduling with a Fixed Action Model

We use the same frozen Focus action model to compare four scheduling modes on the same 120 episodes (Table 15). All modes use the same history-window length, action-prefix length, and task budgets. Focus dropout during training supports input without a Focus prompt in F-Global. F-Linear and F-Adaptive use the same simulator-assisted completion and executability tests. The former enforces a fixed order, while the latter permits reordering and revisitation.

F-VLM achieves the highest Q-score and complete-task success rate among the four modes, reaching 0.4411 and 30.83%, respectively. Compared with F-Global, it gains 0.0210 Q-score and completes one additional episode out of 120, corresponding to a 0.83 percentage-point difference in success rate. This comparison evaluates explicit Focus conditioning together with online scheduling. The simulator-assisted modes show a different pattern. Under the same completion and executability tests, F-Adaptive achieves a higher success rate than F-Linear, 27.50% versus 25.00%, but a lower Q-score, 0.3785 versus 0.4115. Thus, flexible ordering and revisitation do not improve both measures in this diagnostic comparison.

6.4.3 Task Transitions and Demonstration Coverage

The scheduling comparisons highlight the need to determine whether the physical state at the end of one operation is suitable for the next. Retrieving a bottle establishes possession, but pouring or placement also requires an appropriate grasp and orientation. Closing a door depends on whether retrieval is complete and a hand is available. A direct handoff therefore requires both completion of the preceding operation and satisfaction of the next operation’s physical preconditions. The relevant state includes the objects and contacts in the scene, beyond the robot proprioception denoted by sts_{t}.

This dependence on preceding interactions is also visible in demonstration coverage. We analyze 20,000 original demonstrations across 100 BEHAVIOR tasks, with 200 demonstrations per task. The analysis uses the original skill_annotation, removes navigation, normalizes object categories, and counts support by independent demonstration. Workflow variation appears even within a single task. For toolbox organization, 161 demonstrations open the lid before collecting tools. The other 39 pick up and replace a tool before opening the lid. Fixing tool categories, actions, and repetition counts still leaves 67 distinct orders among 126 demonstrations. In art-supply organization, 199 demonstrations with the same four items and pick-and-place counts contain 70 workflows, including interleaved operations on different objects.

These variations change the history preceding an otherwise identical transition. Picking up a drill and placing it in the toolbox occurs in 30 demonstrations. Distinguishing the two preceding operations divides these examples into 16 history combinations, each supported by only one to five demonstrations. Histories involving a screwdriver and then the drill have five examples, while flashlight-and-drill histories have four. The next operation therefore encounters different preceding actions and held-object states. Across all 100 tasks, reordered identical operations occur in 31 tasks, changes in operation composition or repetition in 57, and interleaved picking and placing in 41. Their union covers 75 tasks (Figure 17). The first two categories require at least ten demonstrations of each alternative. Interleaving requires at least ten demonstrations containing pick A, pick B, place A, place B. Categories overlap.

Across 97 tasks with sufficient history and the same 203,245 operation windows, task-wise counting yields 2,851 adjacent transition combinations. Conditioning on the two preceding operations increases this number to 6,849. Of these history-conditioned combinations, 62.8% have support from at most five demonstrations, while accounting for only 3.7% of window occurrences. Repeated individual operations coexist with sparse coverage of the long tail of preceding contexts. These statistics characterize variation in workflow and coverage of preceding contexts. Together with the physical handoff requirements, they identify the unfinished goals, available support and grasp relations, and required physical states that a scheduler must represent.

6.5 Qualitative Analysis of Cross-Task Skill Transfer and Task Continuation

Following joint training across multiple long-horizon tasks, A2-WLA autonomously reuses and adapts learned manipulation skills in execution states not covered by the corresponding task demonstrations. These behaviors arise from the base policy without the Adapter. We examine execution cases to assess how this capability supports local recovery and whether recovery enables the robot to resume and complete the original task.

6.5.1 Emergent Skill Transfer in the Base Policy

Figure 18 presents three representative cases. The boxing-glove washing task provides the clearest example. While carrying a glove toward the washing machine, the robot accidentally drops it, bends down to retrieve it, and resumes the washing sequence, ultimately completing the task. Although the demonstrations do not include recovery from such a drop, the policy adapts learned object-retrieval and transport skills to the unexpected state and incorporates the recovery into the remaining sequence.

Similar adaptations occur in the other two tasks. During water fetching, the robot adjusts its grasp on an inverted bottle and completes a handover. During vegetable sorting, it regrasps a fallen ear of corn and resumes transport. These cases suggest that manipulation skills acquired through joint training can be reused and adapted across tasks, enabling autonomous recovery in states not covered by the demonstrations. However, this qualitative evidence does not identify the specific training tasks from which these skills originate.

Recovery capability alone does not ensure efficient correction. Without targeted guidance, the base policy may spend extended periods on repeated attempts. In the water-fetching and vegetable-sorting episodes, prolonged retries exhaust the available time budget, resulting in timeout failures despite the observed adaptive behaviors. These cases motivate targeted guidance during recovery. Within A2-MEAS, MetaBrain combines foundation-model reasoning with current observations and execution history to generate corrective instructions. The Adapter translates this guidance into action adjustments, aiming to reduce unproductive retries and help the policy resume progress toward the original goal within the remaining episode budget.

6.5.2 Physical State Changes and Embodiment Constraints

Failures can lead to prolonged retries and directly disrupt the scene conditions required for task execution (Figure 19). Examples include a cart tipping over, a lamp falling into a gap between furniture, and food pieces scattering into the sink. The robot must then re-establish suitable grasping, support, or contact conditions. However, hardware and workspace constraints may place the required recovery actions beyond the robot’s reach, joint range of motion, or gripper capabilities. Such scene disruptions can therefore prevent task continuation when recovery demands exceed the robot’s physical capabilities.

These constraints define the scope of reasoning, diagnosis, and action correction in A2-MEAS. Reliable long-horizon embodied autonomy requires learned policies, system orchestration, motion control, and hardware design to be developed and validated as an integrated system.

The base-model study evaluates a cumulative representation and training recipe, and the fixed-policy Adapter experiments show gains from corrective context on two instance sets. Scheduling comparisons and demonstration statistics expose the demands of task transitions. The execution cases illustrate both local recovery by the base policy and its limits. Together, these studies distinguish improvements in action generation, intervention, and continued progress toward the task goal.

7 Discussion and Conclusion

We treat long-horizon execution as a capability to be learned by the action model, with the agent system providing verification and correction at critical points. The experiments in Sections 5 and 6 examine this division of roles through task performance, action-model design, and grounded correction.

7.1 Simple Action Models and Room for Improvement

A striking result is how far a relatively simple action architecture can go. A2-WLA augments a vision-language-action policy with motion-aware history and a latent world model that predicts future visual features. Before adding agent-driven correction, its task-specialized configuration reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset, approximately 2.21×2.21\times the 0.2605 public score of RLC, the 2025 competition winner (Table 8). Even the shared A2-WLA policy reaches 0.4522. RLC also uses explicit stage-transition logic and recovery heuristics [18]. The strong performance of A2-WLA before agent-driven correction therefore motivates learning more of the required behavior within the action model itself, while retaining the comparison’s limits.

The useful lesson is to strengthen a small set of complementary capabilities by retaining recent interaction history, predicting how the scene will change, and translating that context into continuous control. The component study on Selected12 supports this direction. Adding the latent world model to the action-pretrained baseline raises Q-score from 0.4846 to 0.5183, while motion-aware history and the subsequent data improvements bring the full recipe to 0.5905. The remaining gap between partial progress and complete-task success indicates considerable room to improve temporal representations, predictive objectives, demonstration coverage, and training efficiency within this compact design. Better action policies would also give the multi-agent framework a stronger foundation for targeted correction and reliable task continuation.

7.2 Learning Long-Horizon Capability in the Action Model

Long-horizon tasks involve nonlinear composition because the feasibility of a later operation depends on the physical state and interaction history produced by earlier operations. A bottle grasp that completes retrieval may be unsuitable for pouring, and retrieving one object can change hand availability for the next operation. As analyzed in Section 6.4.3, independently successful subtasks do not automatically compose into a successful activity. Their ordering and transition conditions must be represented by the policy, the scheduler, or both.

This motivates training the action policy directly on long-horizon task trajectories, rather than relying on a scheduler to assemble independently learned subtasks. The policy can learn recurring dependencies between operations from these trajectories. Its online decisions still depend on a finite observation window, so long-horizon training does not give it complete memory of the episode. The shared execution record and task-level reasoning supply complementary context. The sparse coverage of preceding contexts in the demonstration analysis further emphasizes the need for training data that preserve cross-step dependencies and cover different ways of reaching a task transition.

Stronger foundation models offer another source of knowledge for action-policy learning. In our implementation, MetaBrain generates corrective instructions that train the correction encoder and adapter, while the original A2-WLA parameters remain frozen. The current results evaluate the learned correction interface. A further direction is to distill broader task reasoning and successful corrected executions into the main action-policy weights, which could reduce the need for repeated deliberation.

The agent system supports this learned capability through verification and correction at critical execution points. It checks progress and physical feasibility, diagnoses deviations, and supplies grounded corrective context through the Adapter. The action model continues to generate the actions needed for the remaining activity. The fixed-policy Adapter experiments demonstrate the value of this complementary role. System-level feedback adjusts execution while the underlying model weights remain unchanged. Recovery is useful when the corrected state allows the policy to continue the unfinished activity.

The 100-task analysis identifies where this division of roles must improve reliability. The system succeeds at least once on 88 tasks, but only 11 tasks succeed in all ten evaluated instances. High Q-scores also coexist with low complete-task success, as in food storage. Further development therefore requires both broader long-horizon competence in the action model and effective verification and correction at points where execution departs from the task goal.

7.3 Limitations and Future Directions

The current correction process pauses execution for diagnosis, which limits its use for events that demand immediate reactions. We prioritize scaling and diversifying interaction data so that the action model learns how contact states evolve and how to respond to deviations from visual observations and execution history. Training trajectories should cover varied object properties, contact configurations, and both successful and failed attempts, including recovery and subsequent task continuation. Together with faster interaction between reasoning and control, this data-driven approach aims to strengthen timely responses within the learned policy.

Correction training uses deviations generated at demonstration states, whereas deployed policies encounter failures that alter object arrangements and grasp configurations. Collecting these execution states and their subsequent outcomes would extend supervision to the situations in which correction is actually needed. This calls for a data pipeline that links failure detection, corrective instructions, and the success or failure of the remaining task.

Current quantitative evaluations focus on household simulation. Additional Adapter tests examine cross-task generalization, while real-robot studies cover short-horizon manipulation and sequential coffee preparation. Future work will expand coverage to more task families, robot embodiments, and physical environments, and assess the consistency of performance gains across independent training and evaluation runs. Evaluation will continue to report both goal satisfaction and complete-task success to assess how improvements in individual operations contribute to reliable end-to-end execution.

7.4 Conclusion

We present A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework that connects MetaBrain, grounding agents, and A2-WLA through code as a scaling interface. The learned correction encoder and adapter absorb MetaBrain-generated guidance during training and convert fresh corrective intent and spatial evidence into action adjustments while keeping model parameters fixed during deployment. On 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 tasks, the system achieves a Q-score of 0.6411 and a complete-task success rate of 45.40%, with at least one successful episode on 88 tasks. The accompanying training and evaluation infrastructure supports iteration across this broad task set, and coffee preparation tests a history-conditioned recovery variant on a real robot. Our approach combines long-horizon capability learned within the action model with system-level verification and correction at critical points. Further progress depends on strengthening both the learned continuity of execution and the effectiveness of targeted intervention. We will release models, training scripts, and evaluation tools to support research on this approach.

Data availability

The BEHAVIOR-1K challenge demonstrations used in this work are publicly available from the official benchmark project[26]. Correction supervision is constructed from these demonstrations using the procedure in Section 2.5. The planned code release includes scripts for constructing correction supervision and training the models on these data. The source dataset remains available through its official distribution.

Code availability

We will progressively open-source the complete A2-MEAS solution at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/A2MEAS. The planned releases cover multi-agent orchestration, the A2-WLA model and trained checkpoints, training scripts for the action model and correction interface, data-processing code for the official BEHAVIOR demonstrations, and the optimized training, execution and evaluation infrastructure. Each release will specify its version, configuration and dependencies.
